title: Will They Reveal Their “Qualification”?
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement. Letter-specific notes: 1. This letter reproduces serious allegations concerning named individuals, a missing person, illicit-liquor activity and a government tender. They remain allegations, court statements and newspaper reports attributed exactly to the source; this archival translation does not independently establish them as fact. 2. The tender-company name is transliterated from the audited Tamil form `இன்ஜெனரி டெக்னாலஜீஸ் சொல்யூஷன்ஸ்`; no outside corporate spelling is substituted. 3. Figures including ₹200 crore, ₹25 crore, less than ₹8 lakh, ₹20,000 per day and the five-year period are preserved as stated in the source report. 4. The *Thiruvilaiyadal* / Dharumi reference is retained because the minister's quoted analogy is central to Kalaignar's response; no added plot summary beyond what the source itself provides is inserted.
paragraphs: Since 2011 we have repeatedly seen reports appear in newspapers alleging wrongdoing by ministers in the Tamil Nadu Cabinet; the Chief Minister, left with no alternative, taking action against some of them and presenting herself as having removed those facing accusations; and, for some “important” reason or other, permitting certain ministers accused of wrongdoing to continue without action. Many ministers accused of wrongdoing have been removed from the Cabinet.

Although I have continued to receive complaints about several ministers, for the very purpose of avoiding personal attacks against them I have refrained even from writing my question-and-answer section for the past few weeks. But despite a succession of allegations concerning the Transport Minister, no action has so far been taken by those above him. Here are some of the details that have already appeared in newspapers.

Gokul, also known as Kamatchi Periyasamy, was the adopted son of the couple Ramalingam and Deivanai of Periyakulathupalayam, Vengamedu, Karur. He studied at Hindusthan College in Coimbatore and worked in a call centre. While studying he fell in love with and married a Coimbatore woman named Gowri Santhini. After Ramalingam's death, Deivanai lived with her foster son Gokul. Deivanai owned 3.5 acres of ancestral land on the Karur–Salem bypass road worth several crores of rupees.

The source recounts that on 3 June 2011, while Gokul was travelling from Coimbatore to Karur, a group abducted him in a car, made him drink alcohol, obtained his signatures on blank papers and appropriated his property. Gokul complained to the Karur District Crime Branch police on 19 September 2011. Police registered a case against Natarajan, Karuppannan, Prabhu, Periyasamy and Mohanraj. After that, the letter says, no investigation took place.
In a statement Gokul gave before the Karur court on 5 January, he alleged:

“On 3 June 2011 they abducted me. Minister Senthil Balaji's younger brother Ashok came there. He phoned the minister and handed the phone to me. Senthil Balaji, speaking from the other end, said: ‘You orphaned fellow, why do you need so much property? If you do not listen to what I say, I will pour acid on you and burn you.’ They confined and tortured me for two weeks. They took me to the Karur Sub-Registrar's office, threatened me into signing and had my properties conveyed into their names. They did not give me any money.”
After giving that statement, the letter says, there was no information about where Gokul went or what happened to him; it was not known whether he was alive.

Although Gokul's confidential statement named the Transport Minister and his brother among those he accused of abducting him, the police did not add their names to the case. DMK Head Executive Committee member and advocate Maniraj filed a petition in the Karur court seeking their inclusion.

The case had been proceeding for many months. What happened to Gokul after giving his statement remained unknown. It was alleged that ruling-party members were using their authority to intimidate people and trying to make the case disappear. The government had given no explanation regarding these allegations against Minister Balaji. Yet it was a person facing allegations of this kind, the letter notes, who questioned the “qualification” of Thalapathi M.K. Stalin, leader of the DMK Legislature Party.

Another newspaper report said that an autorickshaw painted in AIADMK colours and bearing the Transport Minister's name was roaming the streets of Erode without a number plate, while transport-department officials struggled to take action. Was even that report explained? No.
An interview with BJP Tamil Nadu president Pon. Radhakrishnan appeared in the newspapers on 12 March 2013. He said:

“A gang in Karur is engaged in manufacturing spurious liquor. People arrested in a liquor case four years ago are connected with this gang. Complaints say they are involved not only in distilling illicit liquor but in manufacturing counterfeit brandy and whisky. It cannot be brushed aside that people here suspect a connection between Minister Senthil Balaji and this gang. The Tamil Nadu government must pay special attention to this issue.”

Did the government pay attention accordingly? Does the government have a responsibility to explain whether the information linking Minister Balaji with those accused of illicit liquor production is true and remove the doubt, or does it not?

Those reports came some weeks ago. But on the front page of the Times of India dated 28 March 2013, a report appeared in large type. As summarised in the Tamil source, it said that a contract worth ₹200 crore for installing electronic ticketing machines in Transport Department buses had been given to a company with no experience in manufacturing ticket machines. According to the Registrar of Companies website, the source report said, the company did not possess the necessary qualifications. The company installing the machines would receive more than ₹20,000 per day, and the contract would continue for five years. The Times of India, the letter says, had documents relating to the matter.

The company that received the tender had been incorporated only on 24 January 2013—the very date associated in the source with the tender process. The tender date had been postponed twice: first from 31 December 2012 to 18 January 2013, and then to 24 January 2013.

One of the principal conditions for submitting a tender was said to be that the bidder should have assets worth ₹25 crore. But documents allegedly showed that this company's assets were less than ₹8 lakh. Although an official scrutiny committee had pointed out deficiencies concerning the company, reports said the tender was still awarded to it. Many of the documents the company submitted were said to have been handwritten contrary to the rules, and the scrutiny committee was also said to have commented on the company's lack of qualification.
Those who applied for the tender but did not receive it complained to the department that two of the three members of the company now awarded the contract had previously been blacklisted.

The Times of India, which wrote about the matter in detail, reported that it had asked a department official for an explanation; although the official declined to answer specific questions, the official said no wrongdoing had occurred.

Because a major English newspaper had published such detailed allegations concerning a government department, Thalapathi M.K. Stalin, as leader of the DMK Legislature Party, sought an explanation from the government in the Assembly itself on the 28th. He was not permitted to speak about it there, and DMK members walked out. Much later, even the DMK's request for an explanation was deleted from the Assembly record.

If the AIADMK government's action was proper, why could the explanation given yesterday not have been given in the Assembly on that very day? Why deny even permission to speak? The minister offered an explanation only four days after the allegation appeared in the newspaper. Why the delay? Would not the public entertain many kinds of suspicion because of it?

A very serious allegation about the government appeared in an English newspaper on the basis, it said, of documents in its possession. The government should properly answer it. It would not be right, instead, to contemplate filing a defamation case against the newspaper for asking how it published the information. Because the government files defamation cases over everything and attempts to immobilise those who point out wrongdoing, the letter argues, many governmental faults go unexposed. If a government is honest, its duty is to answer legitimate allegations satisfactorily—not intimidate people through litigation.

When an allegation on the front page of a major newspaper circulated throughout India is raised not only by the DMK but by the CPI(M), the Communist Party of India and Puthiya Tamilagam, a responsible minister ought to answer. Saying instead that they have “no qualification,” comparing them to Dharumi in Thiruvilaiyadal claiming as his own a poem someone else had written in a hall, and dismissing the allegation as something written by “a few germs” is not the “qualification” expected of a minister; nor does it contribute to the dignity that should be preserved in the Assembly.

Some newspapers reported the minister as having said in the Assembly: “If Dakshinamurthy changes his name to Karunanidhi, will his inborn nature change?” From that alone, the people of the country can understand the “qualification” of an AIADMK minister.

Finally, one explanation from the minister. The minister admits that this particular tender was awarded to a company called Ingenery Technologies Solutions, as rendered from the source name. When was this company started? When was the tender issued? The tender condition required three years of experience—why was that ignored? The minister says the company had earlier operated under some other name. If it had operated under another name, should it not have sought the tender under that company's name? Why was the government's own condition relaxed?
Will the minister or the Chief Minister answer these questions? Will they reveal their own “qualification”?
With affection, M.K. 3 April 2013
